newsitem.title: USA: Stocks bounce back from Friday's losses.
newsitem.headline: Stocks bounce back from Friday's losses.

text.p: Wall Street stocks powered ahead Monday in a sharp turnaround from Friday when comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan rattled financial markets worldwide.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 47.34 points at 6,429.28, bouncing back from a loss Friday of 55.16 points. In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 16-7 on active volume of 215 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

At one time Friday, the world's most closely watched stock index tumbled nearly 145 points -- its steepest drop since July 15 when it tumbled 161.05 points -- on Greenspan's warning about "irrational exuberance" in asset markets.
Wall Street's nerves also were soothed by comments from leading officials, including Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, that Friday's reaction to Greenspan's remarks was overdone.

The Fed chief's comment in a speech delivered Thursday night, was viewed as a hint that the central bank might boost interest rates to temper the explosive rise in stock prices, which saw the 30-stock Dow index rise 500 points in November.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 18.93 points to 1,306.61, and the American Stock Exchange index gained 3.61 to 589.31.
"We're back to where we were," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "I think just about everyone has gotten over their Greenspan shock."
Wall Street had time to reflect over the weekend on Greenspan's rhetorical questions regarding topics like "irrational exuberance" in the markets.
Johnson said investors had apparently concluded the Fed chairman would not "use the blunt instrument of interest rate policy" to quell the market's rise.

"The 'buy on the dip' mentality is just as strong as ever," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "The only negative is that volume in both the primary and secondary names is lackluster."
"It's going to take heavy volume to bust us out of the trading range we're in," he said.
Technology issues were among the strongest performers.
Microsoft Corp. surged 3-5/8 to 80 and Dell Computer Corp. jumped 2-3/8 to 59-1/8. Both companies were trading for the first time since they formally split their shares.

The oil sector was one of the market's few weak spots, with Exxon Corp. and Texaco Inc., hurt by a drop in crude prices following news that the United Nations had accepted a deal allowing Iraq to resume limited oil exports.
Exxon fell 3/4 to 94-1/8 and Texaco eased 1/2 to 99.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, January crude oil was off 52 cents at $25.10 a barrel.
The most active NYSE issue was Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp., which rose 1 to 16-1/4 on its deal to be acquired by Homestake Mining Co.
Homestake's $2.3 billion offer, which values Santa Fe at $17.42 per share, followed an unsolicited $2 billion offer made last week by Newmont Mining Corp.
Homestake Mining fell 7/8 to 14-3/4, while Newmont Mining fell 1/2 to 46-3/8.
